name: bluewater-shorts-83-92
lines: This family has hired four contractors this week.
A painter. A paving company. A locksmith. And a dentist.
They are not real. It's a stock photo. Anyone can buy it.
And your customer has seen them before.
So when she lands on your website, she doesn't see a business.
She sees a template. And she wonders what else isn't real.
Now look at this one. Blurry. A bit crooked. A real guy on a real floor.
It's a worse photo. And she trusts it more.
Real beats pretty. Every time.
This week, take ten photos of your own work. And put your own face on the front page.
She is trying to pay this man. He's making it hard.
The job is done. It looks great. She's happy.
So she asks. How do I pay you? Cheque or cash, he says.
She has not written a cheque since two thousand and nine.
So she hunts for the chequebook. Then she drives to the bank. Then she forgets.
He waits three weeks for money she wanted to give him on day one.
And that's her last memory of him. A chore.
Now the same job. He holds out his phone. She taps her card.
Paid in four seconds. Before the truck is even packed.
Make paying you the easiest part of the job.
He just lost a job, standing ten feet away from it.
He has cut her grass every week for three years.
She likes him. She trusts him. She'd hire him for anything.
Then one Saturday, a different truck pulls in. Gutter cleaning.
He stares at it. I do gutters, he says.
You do? You never told me.
Three years. She never knew, because he never said it.
Your customers think you do one thing. The thing they hired you for.
So put it on every invoice. One line. We also do this, this, and this.
The easiest customer to win is the one you already have.
This email address just lost a job.
She asked two fence companies for a quote.
Same fence. Almost the same price.
The first quote came from an address with the business name in it.
The second came from fence king eighty eight, at a free email account.
One looks like a company. One looks like a guy who might vanish.
And she's about to hand over a deposit. Who would you pick?
An address at your own business name takes about ten minutes to set up.
After that it's on every quote, every invoice, every reply.
It's a small thing. She notices.
A customer wrote to this business four months ago. Nobody has opened it.
She found his page. She saw the photos. She liked the work.
So she tapped message. Hi. Do you build stone patios?
And then, nothing. One day. Three days. A week.
He's not rude. He just forgot that inbox exists.
He thinks customers call. A lot of them don't. They message, wherever they found you.
So she booked someone else. The one who answered in an hour.
Tonight, open every inbox you have. Your page. Your listing. Your website form.
Answer them. Or switch them off.
An inbox nobody checks is a locked door with an open sign on it.
This woman sent him four customers. Then she stopped.
Her name is June. He fixed her fence two years ago.
She told her sister. Her neighbour. Her boss. A guy at the gym.
Four jobs. And he never asked where they came from.
So June never heard a word. Not a thank you. Not a text.
And slowly, she stopped saying his name.
She wasn't angry. She just thought, why bother?
Now rewind. Every new customer, he asks one thing. Who sent you?
Then he texts June. Thank you. Your sister just booked. I owe you one.
People repeat what gets noticed. Thank the person who sent them. Every time.
He did perfect work. She gave him three stars.
New tile. Straight lines. Not one mistake.
Then he packed up fast. He was late for the next job.
Dust on the counter. Footprints in the hall. A coffee cup on the stairs.
She spent an hour cleaning up after the man she paid to fix her house.
So when her friend asked, how was he? She said, good. But.
Nobody can judge your tile. Everybody can judge a mess.
The last ten minutes is the only part of the job she fully understands.
So sweep. Wipe. Walk her through it. Then leave.
The job isn't finished until the cleanup is.
She needs him today. She lives eleven minutes away. She will never call.
There's a wasp nest over her front door.
She searches. She finds him. Good photos. Good reviews.
But his website says one thing. Serving the city.
She lives one town over. Is that the city? She doesn't know.
And she's not going to call and ask. Nobody does.
So she picks the next one down. His site lists her town, by name.
The first guy would have been there in eleven minutes.
List every town you serve. By name. On your website and on your listing.
People don't call to ask. They call the one who already answered.
He hasn't been to this house in three years. Watch what he does.
She calls. Hi. You stained my deck a while back?
Most guys say, uh, remind me. What's the address?
He says, the grey house on the corner. Is Pickles still digging under the fence?
She laughs. She is not calling anyone else now.
He doesn't have a great memory. He has a notebook.
After every job, two minutes. The colour. Where to park. The dog's name.
Three years later, it takes him ten seconds to sound like he never forgot her.
You don't need software for this. The notes app on your phone works.
Write it down today. It's the cheapest way to be remembered.
He's about to lose this job by insulting someone who isn't even here.
She has two quotes. His, and a cheaper one.
So she asks him. Why are you more?
And he says it. That guy? He's a hack. He cuts corners. Half his jobs fall apart.
He thinks he just won. Watch her face.
She's thinking, is this how he talks about his customers?
Now try it the other way. Why are you more?
I can't speak for him. Here's what's in my price. Two coats. Full cleanup. And I come back if anything fails.
Same price. Same job. But now she's looking at a professional.
Never sell by tearing someone down. Sell what you do.
